extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (authors and referees) submitting computer-assisted proofs to the Annals of Mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for submission and editorial/refereeing treatment of computer-assisted mathematical proofs to the Annals of Mathematics, specifying what parts will be refereed, what must be provided, and how computer-derived components should control sources of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of computer-assisted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-assisted proofs of exceptionally important mathematical theorems will be considered by the Annals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the scope: only proofs of exceptional importance are generally considered when computer assistance is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing of the human part
rubrics_metrics.description: The human part of the proof, which reduces the original mathematical problem to one tractable by the computer, will be refereed for correctness in the traditional manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reduction/analysis done by the authors (the non-computer portion) is subject to the journal's usual peer review for mathematical correctness and exposition; this portion will be printed in the journal issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination standard for the computer part
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer part may not be checked line-by-line, but will be examined for the methods by which the authors have eliminated or minimized possible sources of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than exhaustive code vetting, referees/editors will evaluate the methodology used to control errors introduced by computation (see concrete examples below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required methods to eliminate or minimize specific error sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must demonstrate how they have eliminated or minimized possible sources of error: (e.g., round-off error eliminated by interval arithmetic, programming error minimized by transparent surveyable code and consistency checks, computer error minimized by redundant calculations, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples provided: use of interval arithmetic to address round-off errors; transparent/surveyable code plus consistency checks to reduce programming errors; redundant calculations to detect/minimize computer errors. The parenthetical defines 'surveyable' as: 'Surveyable means that an interested person can readily check that the code is essentially operating as claimed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyability requirement for code
rubrics_metrics.description: Code should be 'transparent' and 'surveyable' so that an interested person can readily check that the code is essentially operating as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyability is explicitly defined on the page; authors should structure and document code to allow external checking of its essential operation rather than expecting line-by-line reproof by referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival and provision of code, documentation, and output
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors will provide the computer code, documentation necessary to understand it, and the computer output, all of which will be maintained on the Annals of Mathematics website online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal will host and maintain the computational artifacts (code, docs, outputs) online alongside the published human part so that others can inspect and reproduce the computational components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication practice for papers with computational parts
rubrics_metrics.description: We will print the human part of the paper in an issue of the Annals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the human explanatory/reductive portion is published in the printed journal, the computational artifacts are provided online (see archival requirement).
